summary: When a Carrier Grade NAT or application proxy sits in the path, a remote server cannot tell which host behind a shared IP address sent a packet. This document collects potential solutions for revealing a host identifier (HOST_ID) unique to each host. It analyzes them without recommending one.

eli5.summary: When many people share one return address, a server cannot tell them apart. This looks at ways to add a personal tag.

questions: identifying hosts behind shared ip address
subtitle: Evaluating methods to identify individual hosts sharing a public IP address.

tldr.problem: When Carrier Grade NAT or address-sharing devices assign one public IP to many hosts (to extend IPv4 address space), remote servers cannot tell which host behind that IP is sending packets. Misbehaving hosts get entire IP blocks blacklisted, harming innocent users.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes nine different channels for conveying a unique host identifier: IP header fields, TCP options, HTTP headers, port assignments, ICMP notifications, dedicated protocols, and other methods. Each has different trade-offs in deployment scope, success rates, performance impact, and privacy.
tldr.outcome: No single solution fits all scenarios. TCP options and HTTP headers show highest success rates in practice. TCP option solutions have ~99.9% success with servers. Application-level headers (HTTP Forwarded) are widely deployed. Port set assignment requires no protocol changes but only works for a service provider's own servers.

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: IPv4 address sharing via CGN or NAT

today: RFC 6967 is Informational and does not recommend a single solution. As of 2013, TCP options and HTTP Forwarded headers are the most widely deployed in practice. The RFC documents the analysis to inform future standardization decisions. It has not been obsoleted and remains relevant as carriers continue address-sharing deployments.

sections.title: The Host Identification Problem
sections.content:
IPv4 address space exhaustion forces Internet Service Providers to use address sharing: assigning a single public IPv4 address to many customers. A Carrier Grade NAT (CGN) or similar device performs the translation. When a remote server receives traffic from a shared address, it cannot distinguish which customer sent it. If one customer spams or attacks, the server blacklists the entire public IP address, blocking all customers behind it. This harms innocent users and creates operational headaches for ISPs.

The RFC addresses this by analyzing potential solutions for conveying a HOST_ID: a unique identifier for each host under a shared address. The identifier must be unique per host but need not be globally unique or permanent. The solutions examined range from reusing existing IP fields to defining new protocol options to completely separate mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Many people share one public IP address. When one person misbehaves, everyone is blamed. This RFC lists nine ways servers could learn which person actually sent each packet.

sections.title: Evaluation Criteria and Findings
sections.content: The RFC evaluates each solution across multiple dimensions: protocol coverage (works with TCP only? UDP too? all protocols?), success ratio (what fraction of servers accept it?), performance impact, whether host or server OS changes are required, deployability today, and privacy implications. Key findings: TCP options have approximately 99.9% success with top websites in experiments (low 0.103% failure). HTTP Forwarded header is already widely deployed and works for web traffic. Port set assignment requires no protocol change and has 100% success but only helps a provider's own customers, not third-party services. IP options have poor success (only 50-60%) because routers filter them. PROXY Protocol requires server support and cannot work across the public Internet. ICMP notification channel works but adds traffic overhead and complexity. Ident (out-of-band) is similar with high success but requires separate queries.
sections.eli5: Some solutions work with any protocol; others only TCP or HTTP. Some succeed almost always; others fail often. Some need server changes; others only network device changes. Some are deployable now; others need years of upgrades.

sections.title: Layer-Specific Solutions
sections.content:
IP layer solutions include using the 16-bit ID field in the IPv4 header, or defining a new IP option. Both face problems: the ID field is meant for fragment reassembly and rewriting it violates RFC 6864; IP options are filtered by many routers. Practical deployment fails.

Transport layer: TCP options work well. A NAT device inserts a 16-bit HOST_ID in a TCP SYN option. Servers read it and remember the identifier for the connection. Downsides: only works for TCP, limited option space, and if multiple NATs are in path, the original identifier may be lost. Nevertheless, experimentation shows this works in practice.

Application layer: HTTP Forwarded header (RFC 7239) is the most deployed solution. Proxies and CGN devices strip existing Forwarded headers, inject their own showing the original IP, and servers use it for logging and policy. Works only for HTTP, not HTTPS (cannot modify encrypted traffic), but is already widely used by load balancers.
sections.eli5: IP layer: existing fields do not work well, new options get filtered. Transport layer (TCP options): works but only for TCP. Application layer (HTTP headers): works great for HTTP but not encrypted HTTPS.

sections.title: Alternative Mechanisms
sections.content:
Port set assignment requires no protocol changes. The CGN assigns each host a restricted range of source ports (for example, host 1 gets ports 1-2047, host 2 gets ports 2048-4095). The ISP announces these port ranges offline to partner servers. A server receiving a connection from port 3000 knows it came from host 2. 100% success rate, but only helps ISP-owned services (content providers, internal services). Third-party Internet services cannot reliably use this.

HIP (Host Identity Protocol) introduces a new cryptographic identifier. Both client and server must support HIP, too high a barrier. Notification channels like ICMP Echo send the HOST_ID in a separate packet parallel to the main traffic. Works, but adds overhead and complexity: load balancers may send the SYN to one server and the ICMP to another. Ident (RFC 1413) is similar: the server opens a separate TCP connection to port 113 to query the NAT for the identifier. Works but adds latency and requires administrative relationships between ISPs and server operators.
sections.eli5: Port division: assign each host a range of port numbers (works 100%, but only for the ISP's own services). Notification channel (ICMP): send identifier in separate packet (works, adds delay). Ident: server asks NAT who sent this? over a separate connection (works, adds delay).

sections.title: Privacy and Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
HOST_ID mechanisms raise privacy concerns. A persistent, globally unique identifier enables user tracking across time and sites. Design guidance: keep HOST_IDs local (unique within a NAT, not globally), regenerate them when hosts reboot, and avoid combining multiple solutions (which enables fingerprinting).

Address sharing itself provides some anonymity—actions are unattributable to a single host—but HOST_ID mechanisms reduce that anonymity. Users deserve transparency about what information is revealed. NAT devices should allow users to opt out of HOST_ID injection if they value privacy over service quality.

The RFC does not recommend a single solution because the working group concluded it was premature. Different deployments have different constraints. TCP options fit for operators who can modify servers. HTTP headers fit for web-focused deployments. Port sets fit for ISP-internal services. Operators must choose based on their specific needs and willingness to modify infrastructure.
sections.eli5: If a HOST_ID is permanent and global, servers can track users over time (bad for privacy). If it changes often and stays local, tracking is harder. No single method works everywhere, so operators pick based on their situation.

sections.title: Summary and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC provides a comprehensive analysis without a mandate. Real-world experience shows that TCP options and HTTP Forwarded headers are the most practical for general Internet services. TCP options achieve very high success rates and require only NAT device changes. HTTP headers are already widely used but apply only to web services.

For operators controlling both the NAT and the target servers (ISP's own content, internal services, data centers), port set assignment is simplest and has zero failure risk. For mobile carriers, deterministic port assignment aligns with existing operational practices. For general Internet services, a combination approach may emerge: operators use TCP options where possible and fall back to other methods as needed. The RFC's analysis provides the foundation for future decisions as address-sharing becomes more prevalent and IPv6 deployment expands.
sections.eli5: TCP options work best for the general Internet. HTTP headers for web. Port sets for ISP-owned services. No one solution fits all; operators choose based on their control over servers and tolerance for upgrades.
